assessments.brief: Write a one-page AI product brief for a problem from your own work: the user, the job to be done, the unit of work, one primary metric with a target, two guardrail metrics and three non-goals.
assessments.title: Assignment 1: AI product brief

assessments.brief: Apply the three-part fit check (judgement, tolerance, volume) and the deterministic test to three tasks from your organisation, and recommend AI, rules or neither for each with reasons.
assessments.title: Fit check exercise

assessments.brief: For your product, list the false positive and false negative errors, estimate the cost of each, and propose a decision threshold and a human-in-the-loop mode that follow from those costs.
assessments.title: Error cost memo

assessments.brief: Design a 50-case golden set for your Session 1 product: case categories and counts, five example cases with expected results, a tuning and held-out split, and the scorer for each category.
assessments.title: Assignment 2: golden set design

assessments.brief: Write a plan to calibrate an LLM judge for one quality of your product: the labelling sample, who labels, the agreement statistic, the threshold you will accept and what you will do if the judge falls short.
assessments.title: Judge calibration plan

assessments.brief: Describe the offline evaluation that gates each release of your product and the online evaluation that runs after release, including how you will detect drift and when you will add new golden cases.
assessments.title: Offline and online monitoring plan

assessments.brief: Draw a trust architecture for your Session 1 product with one layer per high-impact risk, and for each layer state the risk it handles and the evidence a reviewer could check.
assessments.title: Assignment 3: trust architecture

assessments.brief: Build a risk register of at least eight risks for your product, rating likelihood and impact, and map each high-impact risk to a layer from Session 3.
assessments.title: Risk register

assessments.brief: Write an incident runbook for your AI feature covering detection, pausing with the off switch, notification, fixing and reporting, with named roles and time limits.
assessments.title: Incident runbook

units.label: Session 1 slides, slide 1
units.text:
From problem to AI product
Session 1 of 3.
Building AI products that people can trust.

units.label: Session 1 slides, slide 2
units.text:
What this course covers
Session 1: deciding whether AI fits a problem, and framing it.
Session 2: evaluating AI systems before and after release.
Session 3: trust architecture, so people can rely on the system.
Each session has slides, a pre-read and a short graded assignment.

units.label: Session 1 slides, slide 3
units.text:
Start with the problem, not the model
A product starts from a user problem that costs someone time, money or risk.
Ask three questions first: who has the problem, how often, and what it costs them today.
If you cannot name the person and the cost, a model will not fix it.

units.label: Session 1 slides, slide 4
units.text:
When AI is a good fit
AI fits when the task needs judgement over messy input such as text, images or speech.
It fits when a good-enough answer is useful and a person can check or correct it.
It fits when the volume is high enough that a manual process does not scale.

units.label: Session 1 slides, slide 5
units.text:
When AI is a poor fit
Prefer rules or plain software when the logic is fixed and fully known in advance.
Avoid AI when a single wrong answer is unacceptable and nobody can review it.
Avoid AI when there is no data or reference material to ground its answers.

units.label: Session 1 slides, slide 6
units.text:
The deterministic test
Before choosing a model, try to write the decision as a short set of rules.
If ten rules cover 95 percent of cases, ship the rules and keep AI for the rest.
This is called the deterministic test, and it often saves months of work.

units.label: Session 1 slides, slide 7
units.text:
Framing the job to be done
Write the job as: when [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [outcome].
The job stays stable even when the technology changes.
Example: when a learner is stuck between sessions, they want a checked answer, so they can keep studying.

units.label: Session 1 slides, slide 8
units.text:
The unit of work
Define the smallest piece of work the AI system does on its own, such as one answer or one summary.
Every metric, test case and cost estimate is counted per unit of work.
A vague unit of work makes evaluation impossible later.

units.label: Session 1 slides, slide 9
units.text:
Human in the loop, on the loop, or out of the loop
In the loop: a person approves every output before it takes effect.
On the loop: outputs take effect, and a person monitors and can step in.
Out of the loop: no person reviews outputs; only for low-risk, reversible tasks.

units.label: Session 1 slides, slide 10
units.text:
Success metrics
A success metric measures whether the user's job got done, such as tasks completed without help.
Pick one primary metric and state its target before building.
Report every metric with a confidence interval, not a single number.

units.label: Session 1 slides, slide 11
units.text:
Guardrail metrics
A guardrail metric must not get worse while you improve the primary metric.
Typical guardrails: error rate, cost per task, latency and complaints.
A launch is blocked if any guardrail is breached, even when the primary metric improves.

units.label: Session 1 slides, slide 12
units.text:
The cost of errors is not symmetric
A false positive and a false negative usually cost different amounts.
Write down the cost of each error type before choosing a threshold.
Example: a wrong answer shown to a learner costs more than a question passed to a person.

units.label: Session 1 slides, slide 13
units.text:
Build, buy or call an API
Call a hosted model API when speed matters and the data can leave your systems under agreement.
Fine-tune only when prompting and retrieval have been measured and fall short.
Train from scratch almost never; it is the most expensive option by far.

units.label: Session 1 slides, slide 14
units.text:
Worked example: support ticket triage
A support team receives 1,200 tickets a week.
Three rules route 70 percent of them: billing, password and shipping.
AI handles the remaining 30 percent, where a ticket has to be read and understood.
A person reviews any ticket the model labels with confidence under 0.7.

units.label: Session 1 slides, slide 15
units.text:
Estimating value before building
Value per week = cases per week x minutes saved per case x cost per minute.
Subtract the running cost and the expected cost of errors.
If what remains is small, the project is not worth the risk.

units.label: Session 1 slides, slide 16
units.text:
Data readiness checklist
Do you have at least 100 real examples of the task?
Do you know the correct result for each example?
Are you allowed to use them for this purpose?
If any answer is no, fix the data before choosing a model.

units.label: Session 1 slides, slide 17
units.text:
Choosing a model tier
Start with the most capable model to learn whether the task is possible at all.
Then run a smaller, cheaper model on the same test set.
Keep the smaller model only if its quality interval overlaps the larger model's.

units.label: Session 1 slides, slide 18
units.text:
Latency budgets
People notice delays of more than about one second in a chat and give up after about ten.
Write a latency budget for each step, for example two seconds for retrieval and five for generation.
Measure the 95th percentile, not the average.

units.label: Session 1 slides, slide 19
units.text:
Common failure: automating the wrong step
Teams often automate the step that is easiest to build, not the one that costs the most.
Map the whole workflow and time each step before deciding where AI goes.

units.label: Session 1 slides, slide 21
units.text:
Assignment 1 and next session
Assignment 1: write a one-page AI product brief for a problem from your own work.
Next session: how to evaluate an AI system before anyone relies on it.

units.label: Session 1 pre-read, p. 1
units.text:
Why most AI projects stall
Many AI projects stall because they begin with a model and look for a problem
afterwards.
Teams that start from a measured user problem are far more likely to ship something
people use.
A useful first step is a one-week diary study: write down every time the problem happens
and what it cost.
The diary gives you a baseline, which is the number your product must beat.

units.label: Session 1 pre-read, p. 2
units.text:
The three-part fit check
The fit check has three parts: judgement, tolerance and volume.
Judgement asks whether the task needs interpretation of messy input.
Tolerance asks whether an imperfect answer is still useful when a person can check it.
Volume asks whether there are enough cases each week to justify building and running a
system.
If any part fails, consider a simpler tool first.

units.label: Session 1 pre-read, p. 3
units.text:
Writing a product brief
A product brief fits on one page and names the user, the job, the unit of work, the
primary metric and the guardrails.
It also lists what the product will not do, called non-goals, so scope stays small.
A brief should state how the team will know the product failed, not only how it
succeeds.

units.label: Session 1 pre-read, p. 4
units.text:
Baselines and counterfactuals
A baseline is the current performance without your product, measured the same way you
will measure the product.
A counterfactual asks what would have happened anyway, without your change.
Without a baseline, an improvement cannot be shown, only claimed.

units.label: Session 1 pre-read, p. 5
units.text:
Measuring time saved
Time saved is measured by timing the same task with and without the product on a sample
of real cases.
Self-reported time savings are usually too high, so log or observe the times instead.
Report the median time, because a few very long cases distort the mean.

units.label: Session 1 pre-read, p. 6
units.text:
When to stop a project
Set a stop rule before starting, such as: stop if the primary metric is below target
after two iterations on the held-out set.
A stop rule protects the team from sunk-cost thinking, where effort already spent
becomes the reason to continue.
Write the stop rule into the product brief so everyone agrees on it in advance.

units.label: Session 1 agenda
units.text:
Session 1: From problem to AI product - agenda
Session 1 agenda (90 minutes).
0-10 min: Welcome, how the course runs, how to use the course assistant.
10-35 min: When AI is the right tool, and when it is not.
35-60 min: Framing the job to be done and the unit of work.
60-80 min: Success metrics, guardrail metrics and the cost of errors.
80-90 min: Assignment 1 briefing and questions.

units.label: Session 2 slides, slide 1
units.text:
Evaluating AI systems
Session 2 of 3.
How do you know the AI is right?

units.label: Session 2 slides, slide 2
units.text:
Why evaluation comes first
Write the evaluation before you write the prompt.
An evaluation turns opinions about quality into numbers a team can agree on.
Without one, every change is a guess, and regressions reach users unnoticed.

units.label: Session 2 slides, slide 3
units.text:
What a golden set is
A golden set is a fixed collection of test cases, each with an input and the expected result.
It is written by people who know the task, not generated by the system under test.
Cases cover common inputs, hard inputs and inputs the system must refuse.

units.label: Session 2 slides, slide 4
units.text:
How big should a golden set be
Start with 50 to 100 cases for a first decision, then grow it.
With 100 cases, a 90 percent score has a 95 percent confidence interval of roughly plus or minus 6 points.
Zero failures in 30 cases only shows the failure rate is probably under 10 percent, by the rule of three.

units.label: Session 2 slides, slide 5
units.text:
Tuning split and held-out split
Split the golden set in two: a tuning split you may look at, and a held-out split you only score.
Change prompts and thresholds using the tuning split only.
Report results on the held-out split, otherwise the number is training accuracy.

units.label: Session 2 slides, slide 6
units.text:
Deterministic scorers
A deterministic scorer computes a score with code, such as exact match, citation validity or latency.
They are cheap, fast and repeatable, so use them wherever the expected result is exact.
Examples: does every citation point to a real slide; is the label correct.

units.label: Session 2 slides, slide 7
units.text:
LLM judges
An LLM judge is a model that grades another model's output against a rubric.
Use judges for qualities code cannot check, such as whether a claim is supported by its source.
Give the judge only the evidence it needs, and hide which model wrote the answer.

units.label: Session 2 slides, slide 8
units.text:
Calibrating a judge
Before trusting a judge, compare its verdicts with human labels on a sample.
Report agreement with Cohen's kappa and its confidence interval, on held-out labels.
A kappa above 0.6 is usually treated as substantial agreement.

units.label: Session 2 slides, slide 9
units.text:
Offline and online evaluation
Offline evaluation scores a fixed test set before release, so regressions are caught early.
Online evaluation watches real use after release, where inputs drift away from the test set.
You need both: offline evals gate a release, online evals tell you when the world has changed.

units.label: Session 2 slides, slide 10
units.text:
Self-preference in judges
A judge may rate answers from its own model family more kindly, called self-preference.
Use two judges from different providers and compare their scores per generator family.
If the two judges disagree by family, report both rather than averaging the problem away.

units.label: Session 2 slides, slide 11
units.text:
Confidence intervals
A confidence interval shows the range in which the true score probably lies.
The bootstrap estimates it by resampling the test cases thousands of times.
Two systems whose intervals overlap heavily should be reported as a tie.

units.label: Session 2 slides, slide 12
units.text:
Cost per correct answer
Compare models by cost per correct answer, not by price per token.
A cheaper model that is wrong more often can cost more per useful result.
Always report quality and cost together on one chart.

units.label: Session 2 slides, slide 13
units.text:
Pairwise comparison
To compare two systems, score both on the same cases and bootstrap the difference.
A difference is real only if its 95 percent interval excludes zero.
Comparing two separate intervals by eye is less reliable than a paired comparison.

units.label: Session 2 slides, slide 14
units.text:
Holm correction
When you compare many pairs of systems, some differences look real by chance.
The Holm correction adjusts the p-values so the chance of any false claim across the whole family stays at 5 percent.

units.label: Session 2 slides, slide 15
units.text:
Regression gates
A regression gate is a rule in CI that blocks a release when a metric drops.
Gate on the held-out split, and call a drop real only when the paired comparison says so.

units.label: Session 2 slides, slide 16
units.text:
Judge prompt hygiene
Hash the judge prompt and store the hash with every verdict.
Any change to the rubric creates a new hash, so old and new scores are never mixed.
Calibrate the judge again after every rubric change.

units.label: Session 2 slides, slide 17
units.text:
Error accounting
Count errors explicitly: a timeout or an invalid output is scored as a failure, not dropped.
Dropping errors makes a flaky system look better than a reliable one.

units.label: Session 2 slides, slide 18
units.text:
Contamination
A model may have seen a public test set during training, which inflates its score.
Check by paraphrasing a sample of cases: a large drop on the paraphrases suggests contamination.

units.label: Session 2 slides, slide 19
units.text:
Assignment 2 and next session
Assignment 2: design a 50-case golden set and a scoring plan for your Session 1 product.
Next session: trust architecture, so people can rely on what you built.

units.label: Session 2 pre-read, p. 1
units.text:
Evaluation as a product discipline
An evaluation is a product decision written as code: it says what good looks like.
Teams that agree on an evaluation early argue less about prompts and more about users.
Each case in a golden set should trace back to a user story or a rule the product must
follow.

units.label: Session 2 pre-read, p. 2
units.text:
Writing good test cases
A good test case has one clear expected result that two reviewers would agree on.
Include adversarial cases, such as attempts to make the system break its rules.
Keep a short note on why each case exists, so it can be retired when the product
changes.

units.label: Session 2 pre-read, p. 3
units.text:
Offline versus online
Offline evaluation runs the golden set on every change, before release.
Online evaluation samples live traffic after release and measures the same qualities.
When online scores fall while offline scores hold, the inputs have drifted and the
golden set needs new cases.

units.label: Session 2 pre-read, p. 4
units.text:
Reading results honestly
Report the number of cases, the interval and the failures, not only the headline score.
Read twenty full examples before trusting any headline number.
A surprising result is more often a bug in the evaluation than a breakthrough in the
model.

units.label: Session 2 pre-read, p. 5
units.text:
Calibration in practice
Label at least 100 items: 50 to tune the judge's rubric and 50 held out to report
agreement.
Relabel 20 items yourself a week later to measure your own consistency, because a judge
cannot be more reliable than the labels it is compared with.
Report the held-out agreement with its confidence interval.

units.label: Session 2 pre-read, p. 6
units.text:
The cost of evaluation
Judging costs money: two judges on every claim roughly double the judging bill.
Batch APIs usually halve the price in exchange for slower results, which suits offline
evaluation but not live answers.
Estimate the cost of a full run before starting it, and stop if the estimate exceeds the
budget.

units.label: Session 2 agenda
units.text:
Session 2: Evaluating AI systems - agenda
Session 2 agenda (90 minutes).
0-10 min: Recap of Session 1 and questions from the assistant's handover queue.
10-30 min: Why evaluation comes first, and what a golden set is.
30-55 min: Scorers, LLM judges and judge calibration.
55-75 min: Offline and online evaluation, confidence intervals.
75-90 min: Assignment 2 briefing.

units.label: Session 3 slides, slide 1
units.text:
Trust architecture
Session 3 of 3.
Designing AI products people can rely on.

units.label: Session 3 slides, slide 2
units.text:
What trust means here
People trust a system when it is right often enough, honest when it is unsure, and easy to correct.
Trust is earned per use: one confident wrong answer can undo many good ones.
Trust must be designed and measured, not assumed.

units.label: Session 3 slides, slide 3
units.text:
Start from the risks
List what could go wrong for each user, from wrong answers to leaked data.
Rate each risk by likelihood and impact.
Every high-impact risk needs at least one layer that addresses it and evidence that the layer works.

units.label: Session 3 slides, slide 4
units.text:
Layer 1: approved inputs
Control what the system may read: only approved, versioned sources.
Anything removed from the approved list must leave the system the same day.
This layer handles the risk of answers built on unapproved or outdated material.

units.label: Session 3 slides, slide 5
units.text:
Layer 2: grounded outputs
Every answer cites the source it came from, so a person can check it in one step.
A grounding check confirms the citations exist and support the answer before it is shown.
When grounding fails, the system says it does not know instead of guessing.

units.label: Session 3 slides, slide 6
units.text:
Layer 3: scope and integrity guards
Sort each request before answering: in scope, out of scope, or needing a person.
Some requests are allowed only in a limited form, such as hints instead of full solutions.
Guards are checked again after the answer is written, not only before.

units.label: Session 3 slides, slide 7
units.text:
Layer 4: human handover
Give people an easy route to a human whenever the system cannot help.
Pass the question, the system's draft and its sources, so the human starts from context.
Measure how quickly handed-over questions are answered.

units.label: Session 3 slides, slide 8
units.text:
Risk register example
Risk: a wrong answer is trusted.
Likelihood: medium. Impact: high.
Layer: grounded outputs.
Evidence: the groundedness score on the golden set, and a citation on every answer.

units.label: Session 3 slides, slide 9
units.text:
Fail closed
When a check cannot run, for example because a service is down, the system should refuse rather than answer unchecked.
Failing closed costs some availability but protects people from unverified answers.

units.label: Session 3 slides, slide 10
units.text:
Data retention periods
Set a retention period for every kind of data, for example conversation text for 30 days after a course ends and access logs for one year.
Delete automatically when the period ends, and log each deletion.

units.label: Session 3 slides, slide 11
units.text:
Consent and purpose
Ask for consent for each purpose separately, such as answering questions and improving the course.
Data collected for one purpose must not be used for another without new consent.
Withdrawing consent must be as easy as giving it.

units.label: Session 3 slides, slide 12
units.text:
Roles in data protection
The data controller decides why and how personal data is used; India's law calls this role the data fiduciary.
A processor handles data only on the controller's instructions, under a written agreement.

units.label: Session 3 slides, slide 13
units.text:
Red teaming
Red teaming means people deliberately trying to make the system break its rules before release.
Turn every successful attack into a test case, so the fix is checked in every future run.

units.label: Session 3 slides, slide 14
units.text:
Pseudonymisation
Replace names with pseudonymous identifiers, such as a keyed hash of the user id.
A keyed hash cannot be reversed by someone who guesses ids, as long as the key stays secret.

units.label: Session 3 slides, slide 15
units.text:
Transparency
Label AI output clearly and show where each answer came from.
Tell users what the system cannot do, in plain words, at first use.
Transparency lowers over-trust: people check what they can see.

units.label: Session 3 slides, slide 16
units.text:
Privacy by design
Collect only the data the purpose needs, and say why you collect it.
Use pseudonymous identifiers instead of names in logs and traces.
Let people see and delete their data, and set a retention period for everything you keep.

units.label: Session 3 slides, slide 17
units.text:
Prompt injection
Prompt injection is text that tries to change the system's instructions, hidden in input or documents.
Treat user text and retrieved text as data, never as instructions.
Test with injection cases in every evaluation run.

units.label: Session 3 slides, slide 18
units.text:
Monitoring and incident response
Monitor quality after release with the same scorers used before release.
Keep a written incident runbook: detect, pause, notify, fix, report.
Practise the runbook once before you need it.

units.label: Session 3 slides, slide 19
units.text:
The off switch
Every AI feature needs a way to pause it quickly, for one area or for everyone.
When paused or failing, show a fixed message with a route to a person.
Test the off switch as part of every release.

units.label: Session 3 slides, slide 20
units.text:
Assignment 3 and course wrap-up
Assignment 3: draw a trust architecture for your Session 1 product, one layer per risk.
Thank you for taking part in the course.

units.label: Session 3 pre-read, p. 1
units.text:
Trust is a system property
Trust does not come from one feature; it comes from layers that each handle one risk.
A risk register lists each risk, its likelihood, its impact and the layer that addresses
it.
Reviewers trust evidence, so each layer should produce something they can check.

units.label: Session 3 pre-read, p. 2
units.text:
Grounding and citations
A grounded answer uses only the provided sources and says which source supports each
claim.
Citations let a reader verify an answer in seconds instead of re-researching it.
An answer without a valid citation should be treated as unverified.

units.label: Session 3 pre-read, p. 3
units.text:
Handing over to people
A handover is a success, not a failure, when the system could not answer reliably.
Good handovers carry context: the question, a draft and the closest sources.
Teams should review handovers weekly to find gaps in the source material.

units.label: Session 3 pre-read, p. 4
units.text:
Data protection basics
Data protection laws generally ask for a clear notice, a lawful purpose, minimal data,
and a way to delete it.
The organisation that decides why data is used is responsible for it; a service that
processes data on its behalf follows its instructions.
Breaches must be reported quickly, so the incident runbook names who notifies whom.

units.label: Session 3 pre-read, p. 5
units.text:
Measuring each layer
Each layer needs a number a reviewer can check: citation validity for grounded outputs,
pass rate on misuse probes for guards, median reply time for handover, and days to
delete for privacy.
A layer without a number is a promise, not evidence.

units.label: Session 3 pre-read, p. 6
units.text:
After an incident
After an incident, write a blameless review: what happened, when it was detected, how it
was contained, and which test would have caught it.
Add that test to the golden set so the same failure cannot return unnoticed.
Share the review with everyone who relies on the system.
